At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Iraq resumes shipping oil for export to Turkey via pipeline
item.description:
Iraq resumes shipping oil for export to Turkey via pipeline

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 11/17/2026 - 20:00
Iraqi oil minister says Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline could reach capacity of 500,000 bpd with repairs and upgrades
An Iraqi government forces member walks next to a pipeline at the Bai Hassan Oil Field, west of the northern Iraqi city of Kirkuk, on 19 October 2017 (Ahmad al-Rubaye/AFP)
Off

Iraq has resumed the pumping of crude oil for export through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan Pipeline to Turkey, as it looks to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

Iraq plans to pump up to 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil through the 960km-long pipeline that runs from the Iraqi city to Turkey’s Mediterranean port, Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Khudair said in a statement reported by the state-owned Iraqi News Agency on Tuesday.

He said the flow could reach 500,000 bpd after “successful completion of maintenance, rehabilitation, technical and operational tests” on the pipeline, which has been shuttered for more than a decade.

Iraq is one of the countries hardest hit by the US and Iran’s competing blockades in the Strait of Hormuz. Nearly all of Iraq’s oil exports exited the waterway before the US-Israeli war on Iran, and revenue from sales contributed to 90 percent of Iraq’s budget.

Restarting oil flows from Kirkuk to Ceyhan is the first step in Iraq’s efforts to reduce its dependence on Hormuz. Baghdad wants to connect Basra, its energy hub in southern Iraq, to the Mediterranean via the Syrian port of Baniyas and Turkey’s port of Ceyhan.

Middle East Eye was the first to report US efforts to revive a pipeline connection between Kirkuk and Baniyas. US ambassador to Iraq Tom Barrack hailed the reopening of the Kirkuk-Ceyhan line on Tuesday in a post on social media.

“Go Iraq, Go,” Barrack wrote.

US Centcom commander expected in Saudi Arabia with dozens of air defence experts, sources say
Read More »

Iraq began reexporting oil to Turkey in September 2025 from the semiautonomous Kurdistan region after a two-year dispute.

That agreement saw the Kurdistan regional government (KRG) and foreign oil producers operating in the region agreeing to allow 180,000 to 190,000 bpd of crude to flow to Turkiye’s Ceyhan port.

But Tuesday’s announcement will allow for oil from Iraq’s federal government to flow directly to Ceyhan.

Turkey has been pushing for a direct connection between Basra and Ceyhan. The Kirkuk pipeline has a capacity of more than 1.5 million bpd.

Energy industry experts tell MEE that tens of billions of dollars will be spent on new infrastructure in the coming years to get around Hormuz. The UAE is leading the way in building pipelines around the chokepoint. 

But recent attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline attributed to the Houthis and militias in Iraq underscore how those workarounds remain vulnerable.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Houthis are 'occupying' part of Saudi Arabia, Tucker Carlson says
item.description:
Houthis are 'occupying' part of Saudi Arabia, Tucker Carlson says

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 11/17/2026 - 21:44
US podcaster says he spoke with Gulf leaders recently, and questioned who could be supporting Houthi attacks on the kingdom
Supporters of the Houthis hold their weapons during a protest in Sanaa against the Saudi intervention in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia's accusation that the Houthis fired at the holy city of Mecca, on 18 September 2026 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

Conservative US podcaster Tucker Carlson said that Yemen’s Houthis are “occupying” parts of Saudi Arabia, and that the American media is not covering the wartime development.

“The Houthis are legitimately threatening the Saudi kingdom right now,” Carlson said in a podcast, released on Monday, where he interviewed American geopolitical analyst Brandon J Weichert.

“They are occupying part of Saudi right now… I don’t know if this is even covered in the American media, but it’s a fact. It’s a really big thing,” he said.

“Are there Houthi forces on Saudi soil right now? There are,” he added.

Carlson did not say where he obtained the information about a Houthi “occupation” of Saudi territory, but the media personality often speaks with senior Arabian Gulf leaders.

The Financial Times reported in October that Carlson visited “certain Arab Gulf royals on their Mediterranean yachts”. Carlson claimed in his interview that he spoke to leaders in the Gulf “this week”.

Carlson has criticised the US defence and intelligence establishment, but he counts Vice President JD Vance as a friend.

Although he has blasted President Donald Trump over the war on Iran and Israel, he told Weichert that he recently had a long conversation with the US president.

'Houthi incursion'

Carlson’s claim follows an exclusive report from Middle East Eye on 2 November, citing western and Arab officials, that the Houthis were launching raids into Saudi Arabia. The sources said that the raids took place in October, but did not confirm that the Houthis were still holding Saudi territory.

Saudi Arabia’s rugged border with Yemen is effectively off limits to journalists. The terrain is a mix of mountains and vast desert. Whole villages there were uprooted after the last round of fighting in Yemen, which saw the Houthis launch cross-border incursions into Saudi Arabia.

US Centcom commander expected in Saudi Arabia with dozens of air defence experts, sources say
Read More »

Fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government is focused inside Yemen’s borders. The Houthis are moving towards the port city of Aden, the government’s provisional capital.

But the Houthis have openly spoken about their territorial ambitions in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis lay claim to the kingdom’s three southern provinces of Asir, Jazan and Najran, which Yemen ceded to Saudi Arabia in the 1934 Treaty of Taif.

The Houthis originated in Yemen’s Saada governorate, the mountainous region south of the border with Saudi Arabia.

The movement takes its name from its founder, Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi and follows the Zaydi sect of Shia Islam. The Houthis recruit across Yemeni society, but their senior leadership claims Hashemite descent, which would link them to the Prophet Muhammad.

Carlson also said that he believes the Houthis are being aided in their war effort by backers other than Iran, who hope to see the kingdom of Saudi Arabia weakened.

“You do wonder who is controlling the Houthis,” he said.

“I think Iran has had a huge effect on the Houthis, but is that the only power that is behind this?” he said.

Carlson did not say who he believes is supporting the Houthis, but Dropsite News reported in October that Yemeni factions backed by the UAE were quietly assisting the Houthis in targeting advice.

item.description:
‘We’re in the midst of a divorce with Israel’: Palestinian American zeroes in on Senator Fetterman

Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Tue, 11/17/2026 - 17:21
The first challenger to Pennsylvania's pro-Israel Democratic senator spoke to Middle East Eye about why the time is right for him to run for office
Pennsylvania candidate for US Senate in 2028, Ahmed Moor, speaks in a video posted on his X account, on 12 November 2026 (Screengrab/@AhmedMoor)
Off

A 42-year-old Palestinian-American writer has emerged as the first challenger to Pennsylvania Democratic Senator and staunch pro-Israel ally John Fetterman in his 2028 Senate race.

It's not too uncommon for US candidates to declare their bid this early. Election campaigns in this country run for at least 18 months before every election, giving voters little reprieve from the ads and media placements. 

Speaking to Middle East Eye on Monday, Ahmed Moor said he is centring three foreign policy priorities. "End the war in Iran. End the war in Ukraine. End the war on the Palestinians."

The slogan echoes the successful platforms of those who undoubtedly paved the way for him: Democratic Socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Democratic Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed.

Though in his conversation with MEE, he did not seem to want the comparison to be made.

Moor is also an immigrant, an Arab, a Muslim, a millennial, a progressive, a passionate proponent of Palestinian rights, and a father of three girls. Sayed has two children, and played up his "girl dad" persona.

Was Moor inspired?

"I'm a man of the left," he responded, sticking strictly to his campaign message. "We're going to have the left-right contest in America all the time. What this campaign is about is the shape of the sandbox. The idea that the Constitution and Bill of Rights is under assault is not a left-right issue. That's an American issue."

'Overdue'

Moor was born in southern Gaza, immigrated to the US as a child, calls Philadelphia home, and has gone back to work in the region since, from Egypt to Jordan to Lebanon, writing for The Guardian, The Nation, and +972 Magazine. 

'Let’s show that we take our ideas and our rules seriously'

- Ahmed Moor

He was also a non-resident fellow with the Foundation for Middle East Peace.

The political novice is running on what has been a winning message this year involving healthcare affordability, abolishing violent immigration enforcement tactics, and getting the influence of money out of the US political system. 

Moor filed his paperwork exactly one week after the 3 November midterm elections, when the "blue tsunami" swept much of the country, including some deep red Republican states, and effectively blew the door wide open for younger outsiders to jump into national races.

He told MEE that he was already "overdue for having been involved". 

"My decision to enter the race comes at a point where the world is more chaotic, less stable. The institutions that we relied on for our mutual safety [and] the reality for Palestinians is dramatically worse," he said. "For Lebanese people, for people in the broader Middle East, for people in Sudan, [the condition] is dramatically worse, and all of that is related to the corruption crisis that we're facing in the United States and across the world."

To that end, he added, the Democrats must ensure that they "clean house" once they assume control of Congress on 3 January, and hold the Trump administration accountable through investigations.

"Let's show that we take our ideas and our rules seriously."

Target: Fetterman

Moor's campaign was launched on the cusp of the stunning rebuke of Trumpism and warmaking in the 2026 midterm elections, but also as Fetterman's approval numbers have tanked, and his former aides have blasted his disdain for his own job.

Moor's campaign website makes it clear from the get-go: "I am running for the US Senate to unseat John Fetterman and chart a new path for America."

Fetterman is in favour of continually arming Israel and Ukraine, and has voted alongside Republicans not to rein in President Donald Trump's warmaking authority when it comes to Iran. 

John Fetterman threatens to quit Democratic Party if next Senate leader is critical of Israel
Read More »

He is expected to be primaried by several Democrats, given his presence has at times become too much of a liability for a party that couldn't afford a single defection on the Senate floor. 

In August, as progressives picked up critical wins in the primary stage, Fetterman told television host and podcaster Jon Stewart that he would rather lose support in his own party than turn his back on Israel for any reason. 

Earlier this month, speaking on ABC News, former New Jersey Governor and Republican Chris Christie predicted Fetterman would switch parties before the end of his first term. 

On Sunday, Fetterman told Fox News he would "walk away" from the Democratic Party if Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, an Israel critic, was elected Senate Majority Leader. 

"John Fetterman is irrelevant," Moor insisted to MEE.

But that's not quite true.

Much of the reason his campaign launch received widespread media attention is precisely because he is seeking to unseat Fetterman, who himself has received outsized media attention since 2022 because of his mental health struggles, his insistence on wearing a jumper and shorts to work, and his inconsistent behavioural patterns with his aides.

Fetterman has also called Moor "very pro-Hamas". 

"Nobody cares. John Fetterman does whatever he wants. What's coming in 2028? I believe it's going to be me," Moor said.

'Divorce with Israel'

Speaking to Fox News on Monday, Moor noted that when he was born in Gaza, "Hamas didn't exist in 1984, [but] the Israeli occupation has been a disaster for the Palestinians, for everybody in the region, and for us Americans."

But he was pressed repeatedly on whether he was "pro-Hamas".

"It's a bad faith question. I'm not going to answer that," he pushed back. "I'm gonna focus on the American national interest."

'The Constitution and the Bill of Rights is my religion. That's my church too'

- Ahmed Moor

The interview was likely just a taste of what's to come from corporate media and special interest groups, should his campaign mount a sizeable threat to Fetterman, who has not yet announced if he will run again.

Mamdani and Sayed were inundated with anti-Muslim narratives and attacks, far more than their ideas were challenged point by point. The messaging grew so loud that advocacy groups warned that Muslims may be intimidated from going to the ballot box or even their places of worship. 

Is Moor ready?

"I'm just not a fearful person," he told MEE. "When I see something I regard as wrong, when I see something I regard as deeply offensive, my impulse is to confront it."

Sayed, like other fresh faces in the Senate, including preachers James Talarico and Adam Hamilton, often spoke of his faith being an anchor during his campaign, thereby bringing together religious values and progressive action in a way few others have succeeded in doing.

"The Constitution and the Bill of Rights is my religion. That's my church too," Moor was quick to point out.

The moral issue that guides him is rooted in Palestine, he said.

"The measure of a good society is how well it takes care of its most vulnerable. I would say that that same framework applies to our global context... Genocide is the worst manifestation of what it means to have our public policy captured by special interests."

Moor is calling for "comprehensive sanctions" on Israel in line with the 1986 law passed by Congress to end Apartheid in South Africa.

"Apartheid, separate and unequal, is inconsistent with our values in America," he said.

That's also why he thinks he can emerge as the main challenger to Fetterman and win.

"We're in the midst of a divorce with Israel. Americans of all stripes, left, right, centre, want an independent country with an independent foreign policy with an independent domestic policy," Moor said.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Thirty years after Rabin's assassination, Israel is again flirting with political violence
item.description:
Thirty years after Rabin's assassination, Israel is again flirting with political violence

Submitted by Lubna Masarwa on Tue, 11/17/2026 - 21:02
In the wake of elections that handed Arabs the balance of power, we are witnessing an unprecedented outpouring of hate speech and racism
Benjamin Netanyahu, then the Israeli opposition leader, addresses the Knesset in September 1993, two years before the assassination of Yitzhak Rabin (Menahem Kahana/AFP)
Off

A week before the recent Israeli elections, I took my 10-year-old nephew to a cinema in West Jerusalem. As we got into a lift in the car park, a young Israeli Jew entered holding an M16 rifle. Other Israeli Jews got in too.

When we got out on the cinema level, my nephew said with a smile: “I’ll give you 100 shekels if you dare to speak Arabic in the lift.”

Speaking Arabic in public has become a real issue in Israel. It’s the subject of panel debates on television, where speakers compete to express increasingly extreme views and to incite against Palestinian doctors, bus drivers and students.

A woman in the mixed Arab city of Yaffa told me she was afraid to use public transport in her town, fearing she would be attacked by Israeli groups.

This past summer, three Arab female employees were dismissed from a fashion store in Afula after refusing to comply with a branch manager’s ban on speaking Arabic at work.

Hate speech and racism dominate Israeli public life to a degree I have never witnessed before. Attacks by Israeli Jewish groups on Palestinians who speak Arabic, or on women who wear headscarves in the street, have become routine.

But the hatred is not directed solely at Palestinians. Secular Israelis attack Haredim, or ultra-Orthodox Jews, for not serving in the army; the Haredim attack coffee shops that open on Shabbat.

Earlier this month, three Israeli women at a daycare centre in Ariel - including the director and two staff - were accused of abusing and beating the infants and toddlers in their care. Calls for them to be executed and treated as “terrorists” went viral on social media.

Former Knesset member Oren Hazan said that he intended to return to politics after discovering that two of his children had been subjected to shocking abuse at the daycare centre. He called for “the death penalty for abusive caregivers”.

While the main target of incitement in Israel is Palestinian citizens, it does not stop there.

Assassinations openly discussed

Palestinians in Israel were subjected to widespread incitement during and after the recent elections, to such an extent that the winning candidates said in media interviews that they now feared for their safety.

Ahmad Tibi, head of the Joint List, said: “When high-ranking officials - such as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the minister of internal security, and others - shout that Arab members of parliament support terrorism, it constitutes a threat to their lives; an extremist might well view an attack on us as an act of fighting terrorism.”

The possibility of political assassination in Israel is now openly discussed. No one dismisses it as hysteria.

The incitement comes from the top, from Netanyahu himself.

Netanyahu claimed that the Arab parties had used foreign backing to steal the recent election. He also posted a statement on Likud’s website describing this as an “attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.

How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians
Read More »

Over the weekend, a Channel 12 investigation revealed that Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, contacted the police commissioner’s office on the eve of the elections to file a complaint against activists from Raam, whose leader, Mansour Abbas, has openly Zionist policies.

Norden reportedly directed police to an intelligence source who was later found to be a former employee of the Prime Minister’s Office. Police used that information to carry out a wave of arrests and searches of activists’ homes without warrants.

The religious Zionist head of the Shin Bet, David Zini, sought permission to wiretap the phones of five Arab members of the Knesset on election day. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected the request.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid accused Netanyahu of staging an “attempted coup.”

It is all reminiscent of what happened 30 years ago, when Israel’s prime minister at the time, Yitzhak Rabin, was assassinated by Yigal Amir, a right-wing law student.

The anniversary of the assassination was marked by Yair Golan, chair of the Democrats party, who said that Netanyahu was “currently creating the conditions for the next Yigal Amir”.

A few hours later, a billboard featuring Golan in Rishon LeZion, near Tel Aviv, was defaced with the message: “Wanted dead or alive.”

Uncanny parallels

Golan was not the only opposition leader to draw parallels with Rabin’s assassination.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yashar, who has been tasked with forming the next government, accused his opponents of leading an “organised attempt … to sabotage Israeli democracy, to incite violence in Israel’s streets, to make the blood of elected officials permissible, and to dismantle, at the deepest level, Israel’s governing and law-enforcement authorities”.

Eisenkot asked supporters to “remember Rabin’s leadership and engrave it before our eyes: in the face of violence, incitement, and the erosion of the foundations of democracy, we will stand firm, without fear”.

When Amir was asked by police why he had killed Rabin, the law student said he could not bear the idea that Rabin’s government relied on support from Arab parties to govern.

Many fear that, whatever the outcome of negotiations between the opposition parties, this is exactly where Israel is now headed

“How is it conceivable that the most fateful decisions for this people should be made in reliance upon five Arab members of Knesset - knowing full well what their agendas are and what they seek? To me, Rabin appeared as a criminal the moment he resorted to that,” Amir said.

He added: “If the government were based on a Jewish majority, I wouldn’t have done this in the first place. I wouldn’t have.”

The parallels with the political situation today are uncanny.

In the elections for the 13th Knesset in 1992, Rabin formed a government based on a coalition of the Labor Party, Meretz and Shas, with the external support of Arab parties.

When Shas withdrew from the coalition, the government became a minority administration, relying on the five seats held by Arab parties to survive no-confidence votes and pass historic resolutions such as the Oslo Accords.

Today, an administration formed by Eisenkot would rely on 19 Arab seats, not five.

Netanyahu and Ben Gvir

Two men played a major part in shaping public opinion in the two years leading up to Rabin’s assassination.

One was Netanyahu, then a rising star in the Likud Party. He consistently delegitimised the Rabin government, labelling Arab members of the Knesset as Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat’s “representatives”, and accusing the prime minister of depending on a “non-Zionist” majority.

About a month before the assassination, on 5 October 1995, a major rally organised by the national camp against the Oslo Accords took place at Zion Square in Jerusalem. Netanyahu gave a speech at the rally, in front of banners depicting Rabin in an SS uniform or Arab attire. Cries of “traitor” and “murderer” rang out from the crowd.

The other prominent figure of that period was a 19-year-old called Itamar Ben Gvir. He appeared on television brandishing a hood ornament ripped from the Cadillac that Rabin used as his official car. Ben Gvir said: “We got to his car, and we’ll get to him, too.”

Ben Gvir is now a cabinet minister responsible for police and national security. And Amir has become an icon for Ben Gvir’s supporters, many of whom are now armed.

Yet the hatred today is much worse than it was 30 years ago. During the Rabin era, hostility was not directed at all Arabs; the term used was “anti-Zionists”, not “supporters of terrorism”.

Today, however, the term “terrorists” is used to denounce an entire group - all 19 Arab members of the Knesset, and everyone who voted for them. Some 840,000 Arab citizens of Israel voted for the Joint List.

Simmering anger

Among the right wing, there is a mindset that could lead some to seek to eliminate Knesset members such as Mansour Abbas, Yousef Jabareen or Ahmad Tibi. They are in grave danger, given that they do not have Shin Bet protection.

But a Jewish political target is more likely, veteran commentator Meron Rapoport argues, noting that the right-wing mindset constructs “tests” for its perceived enemies.

How Israel’s election is further excluding Palestinian citizens from politics
Read More »

“From their perspective, an Arab is simply an Arab - born that way, with little that can be done about it - but a Jew who extends a hand to Arabs is a traitor,” Rapoport said.

This is especially true of a former army chief of staff like Eisenkot: a general expected to fight Arabs, who suddenly reaches out to them and is even willing to acknowledge them as legitimate political partners. Consequently, he could become a prime target.

The right is filled with anger, feeling betrayed by those who cooperate with Arabs. This is government-backed racism. From their point of view, what would have the greatest impact?

In the eyes of the right, Rabin’s assassination halted the Oslo Accords. Historical precedents suggest that assassinating a Jewish leader is more effective. It incites violence and paves the way for it.

Many fear that, whatever the outcome of negotiations between the opposition parties, this is exactly where Israel is now headed.
